design_detail: Retrospective chart review of emergency department (ED) visits at one academic hospital in Colorado (University of Colorado Hospital: urban, about 100,000 visits a year, more than 97% adults), 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016. The unit is the visit, not the person. Visits carrying a cannabis-related ICD-9-CM or ICD-10-CM code were read by trained research assistants, who judged whether the visit was at least partly attributable to cannabis, the route (edible or inhaled), the dose when written down, and the symptoms. Edible-attributed and inhaled-attributed visits were then compared for symptoms, who attended and what happened to them. A second analysis set the share of attributable visits that involved edibles against the share of THC sold as edibles in Colorado in 2014 to 2016, using state sales data and assumed THC contents. There is no group of people who used cannabis and did not come to hospital, and none of people who do not use cannabis.
can_establish: What clinicians at this one emergency department recorded as the reasons for visits they linked to cannabis, and how the mix of recorded reasons differed between visits recorded as edible and visits recorded as inhaled (or, where no route was written down, presumed inhaled), with differences in percentage points and 95% confidence intervals (Table 2). That serious cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, ventricular dysrhythmia) occurred in both groups, although the paper gives no counts (Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph). A rough size of the gap between edibles’ share of attributable visits and their share of THC sold, under stated assumptions about product strength.
cannot_establish: How often a visit follows each form, per person or per occasion: only people who reached this department are counted, with no count of people who took each form and did not attend, so the percentages are shares among visits, not risks. Whether the form itself caused the different mix of reasons: the two groups differed (more women and more people living outside Colorado among edible-attributed visits), the amount taken was written down in 130 of 2,567 visits (5.1%), product strength was not measured, route was presumed inhaled when not documented (135 visits), and the paper reports no adjustment for age, sex, residence, previous experience, alcohol, tobacco or other drugs. What happens in other hospitals or states, to people treated elsewhere or to people who did not seek care. The sales comparison rests on assumed THC content (20% of flower weight, 10 mg per edible unit), leaves out home-grown and illicit supply, and sets one hospital against statewide sales, so it cannot show how much more likely an edible is to lead to a visit than the same amount of THC taken another way. The edible group (238 visits) is small beside the inhaled group (2,329).

sample.recruitment: No one was recruited. All ED visits at the hospital in the five years were eligible (449,031). Visits with a cannabis-related ICD code (9,973) were abstracted by hand, and 2,567 (25.7%) were classed as at least partly attributable to cannabis if the ED provider named cannabis as likely precipitating or contributing, or the inpatient provider did after admission, or the urine drug screen was positive with a documented link within about 24 hours and a condition known to be associated with cannabis (Methods › Study Participants and Coding). Attribution is a clinician judgment recorded in the chart.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults with an ED visit carrying a cannabis-related ICD-9-CM or ICD-10-CM code (Appendix Table lists the codes), and within them the attributable visits as defined above. Visits without such a code were not abstracted, so visits in which cannabis mattered but was not coded would be missed: a check of 4,800 randomly chosen records found 26 with a mention of cannabis that the code search had not captured (all in 2015 to 2016, the ICD-10 period; medical shorthand in consultants’ notes, polypharmacy ingestions), none judged attributable (Results › Chart Review Sensitivity and Interrater Reliability).
sample.demographics: Attributable visits (n = 2,567): median age 30 (interquartile range 24 to 41); 65.2% male; 43.4% White, 36.6% Black, 17.8% Hispanic; 90.2% Colorado residents and 9.8% (252) from other states; 31.6% admitted, 62.5% discharged, 2.1% transferred to a psychiatric facility, no deaths (Table 1). Pregnant: 46 patients (under 2%). Edible-attributed against inhaled-attributed visits: women 51.3% vs 33.1%, living outside Colorado 40.8% vs 6.6%, admitted 18.9% vs 32.9% (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (range 0 to 121); age said to be similar, no figures (Results › Comparison…, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a chart review. Route was recorded in 2,432 of 2,567 attributable visits (94.7%); for the 135 visits with insufficient documentation, inhalation was assumed. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%).
sample.selection_effects: Strong. Only people who came to this hospital’s ED, were coded with a cannabis-related diagnosis and were judged by a clinician to be affected by cannabis are in the data; people who took cannabis without harm, or were harmed and did not attend, are absent, so the paper cannot say who tends to choose which form or how many came to no harm. Attribution depends on what patients said and what clinicians asked and wrote down. The authors note that this department has the second-highest number of visits a year in the state and sits in an area of high cannabis availability, which they say likely raises its rates of attributable visits (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Visitors from outside Colorado are 9.8% of attributable visits and 40.8% of edible-attributed visits (Results › Comparison…, 1st paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Route and dose as written in the chart: the drug-use section of the standard nursing assessment questionnaire and the medical providers’ notes (Methods › Study Participants and Coding). Self-report, not verified; no blood levels. Route was assumed to be inhalation when not documented, because that is the most common route in Colorado (Methods › Measurements, 1st paragraph); the authors say this could have biased the comparison toward greater toxicity in the inhaled group (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Product strength and content were not measured. The paper reports two groups only, edible and inhaled; no breakdown of the inhaled group by product (for example flower, vaporized oil or concentrates) appears in the text or tables.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Route: edible or inhaled (inhaled includes anything documented as smoked or inhaled and every undocumented route). A dose was written down in 130 of 2,567 visits; among edible-attributed visits it was written down in 80, and in 19 of those it was 50 mg of THC or more (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Frequency and duration of use before the visit are not reported. Time between exposure and the visit is not reported, apart from the 24-hour link used in one attribution criterion.
exposure.polysubstance: Not examined. The paper does not describe alcohol, tobacco or other drugs taken at the same time, and no comparison accounts for them. One attribution criterion rests on a positive urine screen plus a documented link within about 24 hours and a condition known to be associated with cannabis; the screen does not show which form was taken. Tobacco mixed into joints is not recorded.

comparison.controls: No group of people who do not use cannabis, and none of people who used cannabis and did not come to hospital. The comparison is inside the attributable visits: edible-attributed (238) against inhaled-attributed (2,329, of which 135 presumed). The sales analysis sets the edible share of attributable visits (10.7%, 2014 to 2016) against the edible share of THC sold by weight (0.32%).
comparison.matching: None. Crude percentages, chi-square tests and absolute differences in percentage points with 95% confidence intervals; no adjustment (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured: previous experience with cannabis (the authors suggest inexperience among visitors as one explanation, without testing it: Discussion, 7th paragraph), usual frequency and amount of use, tolerance, mental-health and heart history (only partly seen in the reasons ‘acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease’ and ‘chronic psychiatric condition’), other substances, and which product was taken.

outcomes.instruments: Manual chart abstraction by four trained research assistants who were blinded to the study hypothesis, after an ICD code search; no clinical scales. Variables: attribution to cannabis, route, dose when available, clinical and presenting symptoms (not mutually exclusive), length of stay, disposition. A medical toxicologist abstracted a random 10% for reliability and arbitrated questionable attributions; 1,111 visits were abstracted twice (Methods › Measurements, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Inter-rater agreement kappa 0.79 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.83), described as good (Results › Chart Review Sensitivity and Interrater Reliability). The symptom groups in Table 2 are the authors’ own groupings; the Appendix Table gives the codes used to find visits, not definitions of the symptom groups.
outcomes.operationalization: ‘Attributable to cannabis’: the ED provider, or the inpatient provider after admission, named cannabis as likely precipitating or contributing, or a positive urine screen plus a documented link within about 24 hours plus a condition known to be associated with cannabis. ‘Edible’ or ‘inhalable’: the route as documented, with inhalation presumed when not documented. Reasons: gastrointestinal symptoms (including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome), intoxication, psychiatric symptoms (acute symptoms such as acute anxiety or acute psychosis, acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease, chronic psychiatric condition such as depression, schizophrenia or psychosis) and cardiovascular symptoms. The outcome is the share of each group’s visits carrying each reason, not an event rate.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Eight symptom groups (some nested within others) are compared in Table 2, plus age, sex, residence, admission and length of stay in the text; P values and 95% confidence intervals are given at the usual level without adjustment. Among the differences that carry the paper’s message, the intervals for cardiovascular symptoms (1.4 to 8.4 percentage points) and acute psychiatric symptoms (2.1 to 12.1) come closest to zero.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Research assistants were blinded to the study hypothesis, not to the route, which they coded in the same pass as attribution and symptoms.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentage of visits with each reason, edible (n = 238) against inhaled (n = 2,329), with the absolute difference (edible minus inhaled, percentage points) and 95% CI (Table 2): gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1% vs 32.3%, −17.2 (−22.1 to −12.2); cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4% vs 18.0%, −9.6 (−13.5 to −5.7); intoxication 48.3% vs 27.8%, 20.5 (13.9 to 27.1); any psychiatric symptom 26.1% vs 24.5%, 1.6 (−4.2 to 7.4); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0% vs 10.9%, 7.1 (2.1 to 12.1); acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease 0.4% vs 4.0%, −3.6 (−4.7 to −2.5); chronic psychiatric condition 0.4% vs 4.3%, −3.9 (−5.0 to −2.8); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0% vs 3.1%, 4.9 (1.4 to 8.4). Recalculating from the printed counts with a standard formula reproduces these intervals to within 0.1 point. Sales (Table 3; Results › Colorado Sales Data by Route of Exposure): 309 times more THC sold as flower than as edibles (range 279 to 325); 219 edible and 1,819 inhaled attributable visits in 2014 to 2016, so 10.7% edible, against 0.32% of THC sold; the authors call this about 33 times the share expected if the two routes were equally toxic.
analysis.covariates: None. There is no multivariable model; visits are not adjusted for age, sex, residence, experience, dose, other substances or year.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The paper says the protocol was approved by the local institutional review board (Methods › Study Design and Population, 2nd paragraph). The comparison of edible against inhaled visits is the stated objective, but no analysis plan is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: All eight symptom groups in Table 2 are shown, including those with fewer edible visits, and several favour the inhaled group, so there is no sign of one-sided reporting. Not reported: counts of the severe cardiovascular events, any breakdown of the 135 presumed-inhalation visits, doses in table form, and whether the symptom groups were fixed before the data were seen.
analysis.power: A sample of 2,000 was calculated to estimate a five-fold higher rate of ED visits for edible against inhaled exposure, assuming a 1:9 ratio of edible to inhaled exposures (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph). The edible group is small for the rarer reasons (one visit each for acute exacerbation and for chronic psychiatric condition), where the percentages are near zero and an approximate interval is less reliable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among visits to one Colorado emergency department that clinicians linked to cannabis, those recorded as edible (238) more often carried intoxication (48.3% vs 27.8%), acute psychiatric symptoms (18.0% vs 10.9%) and cardiovascular symptoms (8.0% vs 3.1%) than visits recorded as inhaled (2,329), and less often gastrointestinal symptoms (15.1% vs 32.3%, mostly cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, 8.4% vs 18.0%) or admission (18.9% vs 32.9%); psychiatric symptoms of any kind were similar (26.1% vs 24.5%). Severe heart events occurred in both groups. Most visits for every reason, including intoxication (647 of 762), acute psychiatric symptoms (254 of 297) and cardiovascular symptoms (73 of 92), were inhaled-attributed, because edibles made up 9.3% of attributable visits. In 2014 to 2016 edibles were 10.7% of attributable visits and 0.32% of THC sold by weight, under assumed product contents. No count of people taking each form, a dose recorded in 5.1% of visits, no adjustment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract concludes that visits attributable to inhaled cannabis are more frequent than those attributable to edibles, although edibles are “associated with” more acute psychiatric visits and more visits than expected. The Discussion goes further: its first sentence says edible products “lead to” more acute psychiatric events and cardiovascular symptoms than inhaled exposure (a causal verb for shares of visits in one department); it treats the 33-fold ratio as evidence that edibles have greater toxicity per unit of cannabis sold, while saying that careful interpretation is required; it explains the higher admission rate in the inhaled group by cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome without analysing it; it cites three deaths linked to edibles, taken from news reports (references 10 to 12), none from this hospital’s data (Table 1 records no deaths); and it recommends limiting edibles to medical use, stronger regulatory oversight and education, which the results do not test. It also states that the main public-health effect may come from the inhaled products, which account for most visits and most admissions. The authors list their main limits (retrospective, single centre, self-report, little dose data, no community comparison group).

timeline.event: Same hospital group: cyclic vomiting presentations after marijuana liberalisation in Colorado (Kim et al., Acad Emerg Med; cited as reference 31, not read).

Label testing of edible medicinal cannabis products in three US cities (Vandrey et al.), cited in the Discussion for inconsistent dosing (reference 33). Not yet readable for this library; will be added.

Poison-centre reports of edible exposures across the United States (Cao et al., Clin Toxicol; cited as reference 6, not read); and a letter on marijuana tourism and ED visits in Colorado from the same hospital group (Kim et al., N Engl J Med; reference 32, not read).

Overview of edibles in this batch, citing a 2015 viewpoint by Monte and colleagues (JAMA, reference 13 here) for the statement that edible products are responsible for most health care visits due to cannabis intoxication; in this study’s counts, edible-attributed visits were 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%).

Same hospital group: mental-health-related ED visits associated with cannabis in Colorado (Hall et al., Acad Emerg Med; reference 19, not read); the authors say such studies did not stratify visits by route of exposure (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
This chart review: visits by route of exposure at one academic ED, 2012 to 2016.

replication.where_it_stands: No second dataset that splits cannabis-related emergency visits by route was read for this batch. The authors say earlier visit studies did not stratify by route and ask for studies that do, with counts of how many people are exposed to each form (Discussion, 2nd and 8th paragraphs). Related papers from the same hospital group cover cannabis-related visits without the route comparison; poison-centre reports use a different kind of data. Treat the edible-against-inhaled differences as one hospital’s record of who attended and why.

funding.funder: Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE), through a competitive grant programme (project titled “The Adverse Health Effects of Edible Cannabis Products”). The paper states that CDPHE was not involved in study design, analysis, interpretation or dissemination (Methods › Role of the Funding Source; Grant Support).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Monte received support from NIH K23 GM110516, NIH CTSI UL1 TR001082 and CDPHE 17 FHHA 96950 (Grant Support), reports grants from CDPHE during the study and sits on the Colorado Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee, a group of clinicians and scientists reviewing the literature on the public health effects of cannabis (Disclosures); Saben reports CDPHE grants; authors not named disclosed no conflicts. No cannabis-industry, tobacco-industry or advocacy funding or ties are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Colorado School of Medicine; Rocky Mountain Poison & Drug Center, Denver Health. The funder is a state health department that monitors the legal cannabis market and convenes the advisory committee on which Monte sits and whose literature review the authors searched (Discussion, 2nd paragraph); it is neither industry nor an advocacy body. Several related papers cited (Kim, Hall, Wang) come from the same group, so the surrounding literature is not wholly independent of the authors. Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study that counts the people at risk: a prospective cohort or linked health-records study of people who eat cannabis products, people who inhale cannabis and people who do not use cannabis, followed for emergency visits and admissions, with amount and product content measured (tested products or recorded labels), time since exposure, other substances, age, sex, residence and previous experience recorded, across several hospitals and states. For the sales comparison, person-level purchase or use data in place of weight of THC sold.

domains.note: No adjustment. Edible-attributed and inhaled-attributed visits differ in sex (51.3% vs 33.1% women) and residence (40.8% vs 6.6% from outside Colorado), probably also in experience with cannabis and in amounts taken, none of which enters the comparison; other substances are not described. Reasons such as cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, concentrated in the inhaled group, shape the comparison of shares.

Route from chart notes and a nursing questionnaire, self-reported and unverified; 135 visits (5.3% of 2,567) with no route written down were counted as inhaled; dose recorded in 5.1%; no product testing; edible and inhaled are the only categories.

Only visits to one academic ED in an area of high availability, coded with a cannabis diagnosis and judged cannabis-attributable by a clinician; everyone in the data has the outcome (an ED visit), and people taking each form who did not attend are absent, so shares of visits cannot be read as risks.
Not an issue for a record of emergency presentations; treatment during the visit does not define the groups.
Route undocumented for 135 visits and dose for 94.9%; handling of other missing values is not described; the check of 4,800 charts found 26 uncaptured mentions, none attributable.

Trained abstractors blinded to the hypothesis, double abstraction of 1,111 visits and kappa 0.79 are reassuring; but attribution is a clinician judgment, symptom groups overlap and are not defined in full, and route and attribution were coded in one pass, so attribution was not blind to route.

No protocol or registration cited; all eight symptom groups are shown, including those favouring the inhaled group, without correction for multiple comparisons; text and Table 1 contain numerical slips (see reporting issues); the 33-fold figure depends on one choice of denominator.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is applied as the closest tool for a chart-review comparison. Confounding, exposure measurement and selection are each judged high (no adjustment, route presumed when undocumented, every participant selected by an emergency visit), and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Against that, the chart abstraction is careful and reported with reliability figures, the results table shows every symptom group including those that run against the headline, and the Abstract qualifies the main finding. The study can be cited for what clinicians at this hospital recorded as the reasons for visits, by route, and for the size of those differences as shares of visits; it cannot be cited for how likely any form is to lead to a hospital visit, and the Discussion’s causal wording and the 33-fold ratio go beyond what it supports.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6788289 (author manuscript; abstract, Methods, Results, Discussion, Tables 1 to 3, the Appendix Table of ICD codes, reference list, grant support and the author-information panel read as text; Figures 1 and 2 are images and their values were not extracted; no supplementary files)

key_findings.finding: Over five years 449,031 emergency visits were eligible; 9,973 carried a cannabis-related code and 2,567 (25.7%) were judged at least partly attributable to cannabis. Route was recorded in 2,432 (94.7%): 238 edible (9.3%) and 2,194 inhaled; the 135 visits with insufficient documentation were counted as inhaled. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%). Visits attributable to inhaled and to edible cannabis both rose each year (Figure 2, an image not extracted).
Attributable visits (n = 2,567): median age 30; 65.2% male; 9.8% (252) living outside Colorado; 31.6% admitted, 62.5% discharged, 2.1% transferred to a psychiatric facility, no deaths.

Reasons across the 2,567 visits (not mutually exclusive): gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 788 (30.7%; 301 people accounted for 440 visits, 1 to 17 visits per person per year); intoxication 762 (29.7%); psychiatric symptoms 633 (24.7%: 297 acute, 94 acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease, 100 chronic psychiatric conditions); cardiovascular symptoms 92 (3.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Reasons for Cannabis-Attributable ED Visits, paragraph; Table 2, last column

key_findings.finding: Edible-attributed (n = 238) against inhaled-attributed (n = 2,329) visits, percentage of visits (difference in points, 95% CI): intoxication 48.3% vs 27.8% (20.5; 13.9 to 27.1); acute psychiatric symptoms 18.0% vs 10.9% (7.1; 2.1 to 12.1); cardiovascular symptoms 8.0% vs 3.1% (4.9; 1.4 to 8.4); any psychiatric symptom 26.1% vs 24.5% (1.6; −4.2 to 7.4); gastrointestinal symptoms 15.1% vs 32.3% (−17.2; −22.1 to −12.2); cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 8.4% vs 18.0% (−9.6; −13.5 to −5.7).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph; Abstract
key_findings.note: Shares of each group’s visits, not rates. Editors’ arithmetic from the Table 2 counts: edible-attributed visits were 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%), 43 of 297 acute psychiatric visits (14.5%) and 19 of 92 cardiovascular visits (20.7%), so most visits for those reasons were inhaled-attributed.

key_findings.finding: Edible-attributed visits against inhaled-attributed visits: women 51.3% vs 33.1%; living outside Colorado 40.8% vs 6.6%; admitted 18.9% vs 32.9% (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (range 0 to 121); age similar (no figures).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors say the higher admission rate in the inhaled group seemed driven by cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome; this is not analysed (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Severe adverse cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and ventricular dysrhythmia, occurred in both the edible and the inhaled groups; no counts are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Colorado sales, 2014 to 2016: 219 edible-attributed and 1,819 inhaled-attributed visits, so edibles were 10.7% of attributable visits, while edibles were 0.32% of THC sold by weight (flower 327,990 kg at an assumed 20% THC, giving 65,598 kg; 21.2 million edible units at an assumed 10 mg each, giving 212 kg; ratio 309, range 279 to 325). The authors call the visit share about 33 times the share expected if the two routes were equally toxic and list the limits: assumed THC content, one hospital against statewide sales, no home-grown or illicit supply, sales not geocoded.
key_findings.locator: Results › Colorado Sales Data by Route of Exposure; Table 3; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: THC by weight is one denominator among several, and none counts people or occasions of use. The overview by Barrus and colleagues (this batch) cites a 2014 Colorado report in which edible units were about 45 percent of total cannabis sales, a different measure that would give a very different ratio.

key_findings.finding: A dose was written down in 80 edible-attributed visits, and in 19 of them it was 50 mg of THC or more. The authors say they were surprised by the low doses reported and note that a typical Colorado joint contains about 100 mg of THC.
key_findings.note: Doses are as written in the chart, not tested; 94.9% of the 2,567 visits have no dose.

key_findings.finding: Reliability and capture: kappa 0.79 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.83) between abstractors; 4,800 random records checked, no uncaptured cannabis mentions in 2012 to 2014 and 26 in 2015 to 2016 (medical shorthand in consultants’ notes; polypharmacy ingestions, no urine screen), none judged attributable.
key_findings.locator: Results › Chart Review Sensitivity and Interrater Reliability; Methods › Measurements, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: retrospective design; exposure mostly self-reported; no community comparison cohort; people attending an ED differ from people who use cannabis in general, most of whom may have no adverse effect; doses not verified; route presumed inhaled when undocumented; one hospital in an area of high availability. They call for a prospective cohort of people who use cannabis and people who do not.

The Discussion summarises timing as described in a pharmacology review (Grotenhermen 2003, not read): after inhalation, effects within 10 minutes, a blood peak at 30 to 90 minutes and clearance within 4 hours; after oral THC, no significant blood level until at least 30 minutes, a peak at about 3 hours and clearance at about 12 hours. It adds that people report longer-lasting and more intense effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping (reports from a consumer survey and a Twitter analysis, not read).
key_findings.note: Not measured in this study; no times were recorded.

reporting_issues.issue: Results and Table 2 print 94 acute exacerbations of underlying chronic disease as 14.1% of the 633 psychiatric visits; 94 of 633 is 14.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small numerical slip; the count (94, from 1 + 93 in Table 2) is consistent. This card uses counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1: in the two cannabis columns the insurance percentages do not match the counts and add to more than 100% (112.2% for the 9,973 coded visits and 107.7% for the 2,567 attributable visits). For example 1,190 Medicaid visits of 2,567 is 46.4%, printed 50.6%; 4,225 of 9,973 is 42.4%, printed 48.6%. The counts themselves add to the group totals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The insurance mix should be recomputed from counts. It does not affect the comparison by route.

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity check puts the 26 uncaptured cannabis mentions at 0.01% of total records; 26 of the 4,800 records checked is 0.54%, and 26 of all 449,031 visits is 0.006%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator is unclear, so the likely number of uncaptured mentions across 2015 to 2016 visits cannot be judged; none was attributable.

reporting_issues.issue: The unit of analysis is the visit. 301 people account for 440 visits for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (up to 17 visits a year), and the chi-square tests and confidence intervals treat visits as independent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Intervals are probably narrower than the data justify, and counts of visits overstate counts of people.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract does not say that 135 visits with no route written down (5.3% of attributable visits) were counted as inhaled; its list of limitations omits it (Methods › Measurements, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the Abstract alone would not know that the inhaled group includes visits with no documented route.

reporting_issues.issue: Acute psychiatric symptoms are reported at P < 0.001; recalculating a chi-square test from the printed counts (43 of 238 against 254 of 2,329) gives P of about 0.0010 without continuity correction and 0.0015 with it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Immaterial to the direction of the finding; this is the difference nearest the threshold among those reported as P < 0.001.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the higher admission rate in the inhaled group seemed driven by cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, and that the higher edible share of cardiovascular visits seems to have translated into more cardiovascular events; neither is analysed in the Results (no admission by reason, no counts of events).
reporting_issues.consequence: These are the authors’ readings, not findings; counts of severe cardiovascular events are not given.
